summary: Describes problems that hosts can have when a link has several IPv6 prefixes and the default address selection rules of RFC 3484 are used. Those rules have been hard to use in practice and can cause communication trouble. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: IPv6 hosts can have several addresses on one link. RFC 5220 explains how default address selection can choose an address that a router filters or that has no route back.

questions: what is rfc 3484 default address selection
why does ipv6 pick the wrong source address
subtitle: Operational problems that can occur when IPv6 hosts choose among multiple addresses

tldr.problem: A host with several IPv6 prefixes must choose source and destination addresses, and default rules can select a pair that cannot communicate.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5220 describes seven source-address cases and three destination-address cases, with brief analysis of possible remedies.
tldr.outcome: Many cases can use the RFC 3484 policy table, but manual configuration is difficult at scale and temporary-address preferences need application input.

today: RFC 5220 is an Informational problem statement published in July 2008. The supplied metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Address Choice on Multi-Prefix Links
sections.content:
A single physical link can have multiple IPv6 prefixes, so a host may have several addresses on one interface. This can happen in a dual-stack network or at a site using both Unique Local Addresses and globally routable IPv6 addresses.

Choosing an unsuitable source address can cause asymmetric routing, filtering, or a missing return route. RFC 3484 defines default selection rules, but RFC 5220 says they can be difficult to operate in these environments.
sections.plainLanguage: A computer with several addresses must choose which one to use when it sends data. A wrong choice can cause the network to drop the message or prevent a reply.

sections.title: Routers, Filters, and Partly Closed Networks
sections.content:
When several routers share a link, a host may choose a source address that does not match the router it uses. With two upstream providers, an ISP may discard a packet whose source address belongs to the other provider's prefix.

A half-closed network creates a related problem: a host may select an address from a network that cannot return traffic from the public Internet. RFC 5220 says policy-table entries can address some cases, while others may also require source-based routing or static routes.
sections.plainLanguage: A provider may reject a packet if its source address does not belong to that provider. A source address from a network that cannot receive Internet replies can also break a connection.

sections.title: Global, Local, Temporary, and Old Addresses
sections.content:
The RFC describes cases involving both global and Unique Local Addresses (ULAs), site renumbering, multicast sources, and temporary addresses. A policy table can help when a host selects a ULA for traffic that must cross site borders or keeps using an old address during renumbering.

The RFC says the RFC 3484 framework cannot express an application's preference for temporary addresses. It points to RFC 5014, which gives applications a source-address preference API.
sections.plainLanguage: Some addresses are meant for local networks, while others can be routed globally. Temporary addresses can help privacy but may be unsuitable for services that rely on a stable address.

sections.title: Destination Address Selection
sections.content:
Destination selection can also cause failures. A host may prefer IPv6 even when its IPv6 route is a tunnel and native IPv4 works better, or it may choose a ULA destination despite having no IPv6 Internet connection.

RFC 3484 policy-table entries can change destination preference in the cases discussed. The RFC also describes sites that need to prefer either a ULA or a global address to distinguish services, even though the default rules do not specify which should take priority.
sections.plainLanguage: A host can choose a destination address that uses a slower or unavailable route. Administrators may need to adjust the host's address-selection policy for the network.

sections.title: Operational and Security Implications
sections.content:
Hosts need information about upstream routing policies to choose suitable addresses. The RFC says routers alone cannot make every source and destination choice on behalf of a host, and configuring policy tables by hand on many unmanaged devices is impractical.

An unsuitable address choice can send traffic through an unintended path or expose addresses through multicast source selection. The RFC says these risks have their roots in incorrect address selection and can be avoided by choosing addresses that fit the site's routing structure.
sections.plainLanguage: Network administrators need hosts to know which addresses work with their routing policies. A wrong choice can expose information or send traffic onto an unintended path.
